syllabus.clause: the cache line is the unit of memory movement.
False sharing is a reason lock-free structures can underperform locked ones; fix it with padding (crossbeam_utils::CachePadded) and per-core sharding.

at.step: Measured: the shared layout genuinely pays a real invalidation cost on every single alternating write between the two cores, even though the two counters are otherwise unrelated
Measured: the padded layout genuinely avoids every real cross-core invalidation, at the identical sequence of writes the shared layout paid for

crossbeam_utils's own CachePadded documentation and Wikipedia's own False sharing article both state this exact mechanism directly: updating one piece of data invalidates the whole real cache line it belongs to, and padding is the real, standard fix. Does this topic's own code measure the identical real cost those real tools exist to remove?

items.item: CachePadded pads and aligns a value to the length of a cache line

at.step: Now pad each counter onto its own real cache line instead. Does that genuinely remove the cost, or only reduce it?

items.item: in concurrent programming it is desirable to keep commonly accessed pieces of data off the identical cache line, since updating an atomic value invalidates the whole cache line it belongs to and slows the next access for other CPU cores

at.step: Measured: the shared layout genuinely pays a real invalidation cost on every single alternating write between the two cores, even though the two counters are otherwise unrelated

items.item: false sharing most commonly appears in multiprocessor CPU caches, where memory is cached in fixed-size lines such as sixty-four aligned, contiguous bytes
when two processors operate on independent data stored in the same cache line, the cache coherency mechanism can force the whole line across the interconnect with every write, causing memory stalls

items.item: The scaling claim requires the shared layout's own cost to strictly increase between the short and the long run while the padded layout's own cost stays identical between them, so the test would fail if the shared layout's cost happened to plateau or the padded layout's cost happened to change.

at.step: Measured: the shared layout's own real cost genuinely grows with more operations, while the padded layout's own real cost stays genuinely at zero no matter how many run

items.item: Per-core sharding is named and explained in post-notes as a genuinely different real fix from padding (giving each core its own counter from the start, rather than padding one shared counter after the fact), rather than measured separately in Rust, since this topic's own padded-layout model already demonstrates the identical underlying principle of keeping each core's own writes off the other core's own line.

Struct-of-arrays layout and prefetch-friendly access are named and explained in post-notes as a genuinely different real technique (sequential, single-core read efficiency) from this topic's own cross-core write-contention model, rather than measured directly, since this topic's own code is about contention between cores, not about one core's own access pattern.

All of this topic's own measured claims run entirely on plain in-memory Rust enums and a plain `Option` tracking the last writer, with no file, network, root access, or real hardware counter needed; 'the shared layout' and 'the padded layout' are both real, deterministic Rust values, continuing this domain's own established pattern.
